title: A Tax Treaty Divides the Right to Tax; It Never Creates One
summary: A tax treaty is an agreement between two countries about which of them may tax a given piece of income, and how much. It cannot create a tax that domestic law does not impose; it can only limit one. Learn its four jobs and you can read any treaty position put in front of you.
body:
A tax treaty is a contract between two tax collectors. It decides which of them may tax a piece of your income and how much each may take, and it can only ever reduce a tax that domestic law already imposes.

Recall

Q. What does mind and management mean in a residence test?

A. In several common-law countries, a company can be treated as resident where its real strategic decisions are made, by the people who actually make them, regardless of where it was incorporated. Board minutes signed in one place do not help if the decisions were really made somewhere else.

Q. What are Omar's six lenses for a structure?

A. Tax, liability, banking, governance, estate and exit. A structure that looks good through one lens and fails another is not finished.

Q. What is a work breakdown structure?

A. The project scope broken into a hierarchy of deliverables, down to packages small enough to estimate, assign and control. Cost codes and the schedule of values hang from it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the moment money crosses a border, two governments can look at the same dollar. One taxes it because the property or the payer is there. The other taxes it because you, or your company, live there. Without some agreement between them, you could pay tax twice on one profit, and a cross-border development that works before tax can fail after it. Treaties are the main agreement that stops that. They also decide the withholding rate on every dividend, interest payment and fee your structure sends across a border. You will not draft treaties. You will be told, by advisers, lenders and investors, what a treaty "gives you". This week teaches you to check that claim instead of accepting it.

What a treaty actually does

In plain English: a treaty is a rulebook for sharing. It does four jobs.

First, it allocates taxing rights. For each kind of income, such as business profits, rent, dividends, interest, fees and gains, it says whether the source country may tax, the residence country may tax, or both. Income from land is almost always taxable where the land is. Business profits are usually taxable at source only if the business has a permanent establishment there, the idea from last week. Second, it caps withholding: the tax a payer deducts at source before money leaves the country. A treaty might cut a domestic dividend withholding rate to a lower figure for a company holding a large stake. Third, it requires the residence country to relieve double taxation, by credit or by exemption. Fourth, it lets the two tax authorities exchange information and settle disputes through a process called mutual agreement.

The professional framing: most modern treaties follow one of two templates, the model convention published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), or the United Nations model, which gives the source country somewhat more taxing right. Article numbers broadly track the model, but every treaty is negotiated and every one differs. Never assume a clause from one treaty appears in another; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The single most important sentence this week: a treaty restricts; it does not impose. If domestic law does not tax a payment, no treaty can make it taxable. If domestic law taxes it at a high rate and the treaty caps the rate, the treaty wins, but only if you qualify and claim it properly.

Who is resident, when two countries both say "you"

A treaty only helps a resident of one of the two countries. Sometimes both countries call the same person resident under their own domestic rules. The treaty then applies a tie-breaker rule: an ordered list of tests that hands residence, for treaty purposes, to one country only.

For an individual, the model order is: where you have a permanent home available; if both or neither, where your centre of vital interests lies, meaning your personal and economic ties; then where you habitually live; then nationality; and finally agreement between the two authorities. For a company, older treaties often used the place of effective management, the place where key management and commercial decisions are really made. Many newer treaties, and amendments made through a multilateral instrument, instead send dual-resident companies to the two authorities to decide case by case, which can leave a company with no treaty benefits until they agree [unverified — confirm independently].

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer keeps a family home in Country A and rents an apartment in Country B for a two-year project. Both countries call him resident. The tie-breaker asks first about a permanent home. He has one in A; the apartment in B is also available to him, so both qualify. The test moves to centre of vital interests: his spouse, children, bank accounts and investments are in A. A wins. Under the treaty he is resident only in A, and B may tax him only as a source country, for example on his salary for work done in B. The order of the tests matters; a wrong order gives a wrong answer.

Say that out loud now.

A treaty only limits tax domestic law already imposes, and only for a resident who qualifies and claims it.

Credit or exemption: how double tax is actually removed

When both countries may tax, the residence country gives relief by one of two methods. Under the credit method, the residence country taxes the foreign income, then subtracts the foreign tax paid, usually up to the amount of its own tax on that income. Under the exemption method, the residence country simply does not tax that income, sometimes while still counting it to set the rate on the rest.

A second worked example, with hypothetical rates chosen only to show the arithmetic. A company resident in Country R earns 1,000,000 dollars of rental profit from a building in Country S. S taxes it at a hypothetical 25 percent: 250,000 dollars. R's hypothetical rate is 30 percent: 300,000 dollars before relief. Under credit, R allows 250,000 dollars against its 300,000 dollars, so the company pays 50,000 dollars more in R. Total tax: 300,000 dollars, the higher of the two rates. Under exemption, R taxes nothing. Total tax: 250,000 dollars, the source rate. Same income, same treaty idea, a 50,000 dollar difference. Which method applies is written in the treaty and in domestic law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The fourth idea: who owns the income

Reduced withholding rates are usually available only to the beneficial owner of the payment: the person who actually has the right to use and enjoy it, not an intermediary that must pass it on. A company placed in a treaty country simply to collect and forward money may fail that test. Devika teaches it fully on Day 4, and Ford shows it failing on Day 2.

How the best do it

The most disciplined cross-border investors keep a written treaty position for every payment that crosses a border: the treaty, the article, the rate, the residence evidence, the beneficial-ownership facts and the anti-abuse analysis, each with a date and an adviser's name. It is refreshed when a treaty changes, when people move, and before every major distribution. A small developer can copy this with one page per payment type, reviewed each year.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the treaty sets withholding and relief, but only if residence and beneficial ownership are real and documented. Liability: a wrongly claimed rate usually leaves the payer, often your own company, liable for the shortfall. Banking: lenders model distributions after withholding and will ask for the treaty position. Governance: decisions must be made where the treaty assumes they are made. Estate: an individual's residence under a tie-breaker can affect how his estate is taxed. Exit: gains on land, and often on shares of land-rich companies, usually stay taxable where the land is.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser qualified in each of the two countries.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure built on a treaty rate nobody has tested against the treaty's own conditions: residence, beneficial ownership and the anti-abuse clause. The control is a written, dated treaty position for each payment, signed off in both countries before the first payment flows.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a table of treaty withholding rates and assumes the lowest number applies. The table is the conclusion of a treaty analysis, not a substitute for it.

Callback

Last week Elias and Ford taught that residence follows where decisions are really made, and that a substance record proves it. The treaty depends on exactly that fact. Every tie-breaker and every beneficial-ownership test asks, in its own words, the same question: who really decides, and where?

Recap

A treaty allocates taxing rights, caps withholding, requires relief by credit or exemption, and lets authorities cooperate. It only restricts tax domestic law imposes, and only for a qualifying resident who is the beneficial owner and claims properly.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of a conduit company that lost its treaty rate.
checklist: I know which treaty, if any, covers each cross-border payment in my structure.
I have confirmed residence for each recipient under domestic law and, if needed, the tie-breaker.
I know whether the residence country gives relief by credit or by exemption.
I have checked that each recipient is the beneficial owner of what it receives.
I have a written, dated treaty position for each payment type.
I have asked whether the treaty carries an anti-abuse or principal purpose clause.
I know who signs off the position in each country.
I review the position each year and before every major distribution.
head: Field checklist
speak: A tax treaty is an agreement between two countries about who may tax a piece of income and how much. It does four jobs. It allocates taxing rights: income from land is usually taxed where the land is, and business profits at source only through a permanent establishment. It caps withholding on dividends, interest and fees. It makes the residence country relieve double tax, either by credit, where it taxes the income and subtracts the foreign tax, or by exemption, where it leaves the income alone. And it lets the two authorities exchange information and settle disputes. Two conditions sit under all of it. You must be resident, and if both countries claim you, a tie-breaker decides. And for reduced withholding, you must usually be the beneficial owner of the payment. Above all, a treaty only restricts tax that domestic law imposes. It never creates a tax, and it never helps someone who does not qualify.
terms: Tax treaty — an agreement between two countries allocating taxing rights over cross-border income and limiting double taxation.
Tie-breaker rule — the ordered tests in a treaty that assign residence to one country when both domestic laws claim the same person.
Credit method — relief in which the residence country taxes foreign income and subtracts the foreign tax paid, usually capped at its own tax on that income.

hostile.q: Your model assumes the treaty withholding rate on every distribution. What happens to our return if the authority denies it?
hostile.a: Then the domestic rate applies and our distributable cash falls, and I have modelled that case separately so you can see it. The treaty rate depends on three facts: the holding company is resident, it is the beneficial owner, and it passes the anti-abuse test. I have a written position on each, with the evidence, signed off by advisers in both countries, and I will share it with your counsel. If any of the three cannot be shown, we model at the domestic rate, not the treaty rate.

title: The Conduit Company That Lost Its Treaty Rate
summary: This is a composite example. A developer routed rent-backed dividends through a holding company in a treaty country to claim a low withholding rate. The company had no staff, no decisions and an obligation to pass the money on, and years later the rate was denied, with interest and penalties.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer paid dividends through a holding company in a treaty country to cut withholding tax, the company turned out to own nothing in substance, and the treaty rate was taken away years later, with interest and penalties on top.

Recall

Q. What is a permanent establishment?

A. A fixed place of business, or in some cases a dependent agent, through which a foreign enterprise carries on business in a country. Under most treaties, business profits are taxable in that country only if a permanent establishment exists there.

Q. What does flow of funds mean in structure design?

A. The path every dollar takes through the entities, from investor to project and back, with the tax, legal and banking consequence of each step. Omar drew it before he drew the boxes.

Q. What is a schedule of values?

A. The contractor's breakdown of the contract sum into billable line items, used to measure progress and pay monthly. It should tie to the cost codes and the work breakdown structure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me today because this failure sits between tax and integrity. Nothing in it was hidden or criminal. Every document was real. The structure simply asserted a fact the treaty requires, beneficial ownership, that the business did not actually have. A treaty rate is a conclusion. When the facts under it are thin, the conclusion falls, and it falls years after the money has been spent.

This is a composite example built from patterns that recur in treaty disputes. The numbers are hypothetical round figures, and the rates are chosen only to show the arithmetic.

1. Timeline

Year 1: a developer resident in Country R owns an operating apartment building through a company in Country S. Country S charges a hypothetical 25 percent withholding tax on dividends paid abroad. An adviser proposes inserting a holding company in Country T, which has a treaty with S cutting dividend withholding to a hypothetical 5 percent for a company holding a large stake. The T company is formed, with a local nominee director provided by a service firm. Years 1 to 5: the S company pays 2,000,000 dollars of dividends a year to the T company, withholding 5 percent. Within days each time, the T company pays the same money on to the developer in R. Year 6: Country S audits. Year 8: S assesses the difference between 25 and 5 percent on five years of dividends, plus interest and a penalty.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Choosing Country T for its treaty rate alone, with no business reason to be there. Running the T company through a nominee director who signed what he was sent. And paying every dividend straight through, on a fixed schedule, so the T company never held, used or decided about the money.

3. Assumptions

The developer assumed that a company resident in T was automatically entitled to the T treaty rate. He assumed a certificate of residence from T settled the matter. He assumed that because the structure was legal in T, it would be respected in S. None of these is safe. Residence is only the entry ticket; the reduced rate usually also needs beneficial ownership, and modern treaties add an anti-abuse test.

4. Incentives

The adviser who proposed the structure was paid a fixed fee to set it up and an annual fee to maintain it, and was not engaged to defend it on audit. The service firm was paid per entity. The developer saw 400,000 dollars a year of withholding saved, which is 20 percent of 2,000,000 dollars. Nobody in the chain was paid to ask whether the T company could survive an audit in S.

Say that out loud now.

A certificate of residence is the entry ticket, not the treaty rate.

5. Warning signs ignored

The adviser's memo said the structure "should" qualify, subject to beneficial-ownership facts it did not examine. The T company had no bank signatory in T; the developer signed every payment from R. Its board minutes were identical every year and were drafted in R. Its accounts showed no expenses beyond the service fee. And the money arrived and left within days, which is the signature of a conduit: an entity that receives income only to pass it on.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was year 1, before the first dividend. Once five years of dividends had flowed through on the same pattern, the record was fixed. No later board meeting could show that the T company had ever had real discretion over money it had already handed on. Ford's rule of thumb: a substance problem cannot be cured backward.

7. Root cause

The root cause was treating a treaty rate as something you buy with an address. The rate depends on facts about who owns, controls and decides over the income, and the structure was designed to avoid exactly those facts in T.

What it cost

The hypothetical arithmetic. The rate difference was 20 percent on 2,000,000 dollars a year, so 400,000 dollars a year, or 2,000,000 dollars over five years. Add interest for the years the tax was late, and a penalty, whose size and whether it applies depend on local law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The developer had already spent the savings on the next project. He also faced a second problem: Country R may or may not give a credit for extra tax S assessed years later, and the time limits for claiming one may have passed.

Real cases worth reading

Courts have decided beneficial-ownership and treaty-shopping disputes in several countries, and outcomes have gone both ways depending on the facts. In Canada, for example, the Supreme Court of Canada decided the Alta Energy case in 2021, declining to apply the general anti-avoidance rule to a Luxembourg holding structure under the treaty as it then stood. Since then, many treaties have added a principal purpose test through the multilateral instrument [unverified — confirm independently]. Read the cases for how judges reason, not for a promise that a structure will survive.

What would have saved it

Run the case forward with one change. In year 1, before the first dividend, the developer asks a single question of the adviser: if Country S audits in year 6, what evidence will prove the T company decided anything? The honest answer, nothing, would have ended the plan or changed it. Either the company is given real directors, its own bank control and a business reason to be in T, at a known yearly cost, or the developer pays the 25 percent and keeps the 400,000 dollars a year as a known cost instead of a hidden liability. Both are defensible. The path actually taken was not.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an intermediate company that exists on paper in a treaty country while every decision and every dollar moves around it. The control is to give any treaty company a genuine business reason, real directors who decide, its own bank control, and discretion over what it receives, or not to rely on its treaty rate at all.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts the withholding saved and never prices the downside: the full rate, interest, penalties and a lost credit. Always model the denied case beside the claimed case.

Callback

In Week 24, Elias and Cole taught that substance outweighs form and that anti-avoidance rules look past labels to what actually happens. This case is that lesson applied to a treaty. The T company's form was perfect; its substance was a pipe.

Recap

A holding company was placed in a treaty country only for its rate, run by a nominee, and used as a pipe. The source country denied the rate for lack of beneficial ownership, five years later. Substance and purpose, documented from the first payment, are the only defence.

Rule 57: Never claim a treaty rate through an entity that does not genuinely own, control and decide over the income it receives; document residence, beneficial ownership and business purpose before the first payment flows.

Next: Sage on The Money: what a treaty rate is worth to after-tax return, and what it costs to keep.
checklist: I can state a business reason for every intermediate company that is not the treaty rate.
Each treaty company has directors who genuinely decide, in that country.
Each treaty company controls its own bank account.
Money received is not contractually committed to be passed on.
I hold a dated memo on residence, beneficial ownership and anti-abuse for each payment.
I have modelled the denied-rate case, with interest and penalties.
I know the time limits for claiming a foreign tax credit if tax is reassessed later.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer owned a building through a company in one country and routed its dividends through a holding company in a second country, because that country's treaty cut withholding from a high rate to a low one. The holding company had a nominee director, no bank signatory of its own and no expenses beyond a service fee, and it paid every dividend straight on within days. Five years later the source country audited and denied the treaty rate, because the holding company was not the beneficial owner. It was a conduit. The developer owed the rate difference on five years of dividends, plus interest and a penalty, and the savings were already spent. The root cause was treating a treaty rate as something you buy with an address. Rule 57: never claim a treaty rate through an entity that does not genuinely own, control and decide over the income it receives.
terms: Conduit company — an entity that receives income only in order to pass it on, without real discretion over it.
Certificate of residence — a document from a tax authority confirming that a person is resident there for tax purposes; necessary for a treaty claim but rarely sufficient.
Treaty shopping — placing an entity in a treaty country mainly to obtain treaty benefits that the real owner could not claim directly.

hostile.q: Your holding company is in a treaty country, but who in that country actually decides what happens to the dividends it receives?
hostile.a: Two resident directors with relevant experience, who meet there, review the company's own accounts and decide on each distribution and reinvestment. The company controls its own bank account, it is under no obligation to pay the money on, and it holds other investments in its own right. I can show you the minutes, the bank mandate and the directors' service agreements. If we could not show those things, I would not be claiming the treaty rate.

rule: Rule 57: Never claim a treaty rate through an entity that does not genuinely own, control and decide over the income it receives; document residence, beneficial ownership and business purpose before the first payment flows.

title: What a Treaty Rate Is Worth, and What It Costs to Keep
summary: Withholding tax comes off every distribution, so the rate moves equity cash flow and after-tax IRR directly. A treaty rate is worth the present value of the tax it saves, less the cost of the substance that earns it and the probability-weighted cost of losing it. Price all three before you build a structure around it.
body:
A treaty rate is not free money. It is worth the tax it saves, minus the yearly cost of the substance that earns it, minus the expected cost of having it denied, and only that net number belongs in your pro forma.

Recall

Q. What is a substance record?

A. A contemporaneous file proving where an entity's decisions are really made: board papers, minutes, who attended, where, and what was decided. It is built as you go, never reconstructed later.

Q. Why sequence the steps of a structure?

A. Because the order of transfers, financings and incorporations can change the tax and legal result. Put land into a vehicle before an approval raises its value, or after, and the tax on that transfer can differ.

Q. What are exclusions in a contract scope?

A. Work the contractor expressly does not include in its price. Every exclusion is a cost the owner still carries, so each needs a home in another package or the owner's budget.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most pro formas show one after-tax return and treat the tax inside it as fixed. Cross-border, the tax is a variable you choose, partly, through structure. Withholding comes straight off every distribution to equity before you can spend it, so it hits cash-on-cash yield, equity multiple and after-tax internal rate of return (IRR) every single year. A developer who can price a treaty position properly can decide whether a structure is worth its cost, instead of building one because an adviser said the rate was lower.

Withholding comes off the top of equity cash

In plain English: before any distribution leaves the source country, the payer keeps a slice for the tax authority. Whatever the rate, that slice never reaches you.

The professional framing: model distributions in three layers. Project cash available for distribution, after debt service and reserves. Then source-country withholding on that distribution. Then residence-country tax on what arrives, less any credit for the withholding. The gap between the top layer and the bottom one is leakage, a word Devika teaches fully next week.

A worked example, hypothetical, with rates chosen only to show the arithmetic. A stabilised building distributes 1,000,000 dollars a year to its foreign owner. Without a treaty, the source country withholds a hypothetical 25 percent: 250,000 dollars. With a qualifying treaty claim, a hypothetical 5 percent: 50,000 dollars. The treaty is worth 200,000 dollars a year before anything else. Over ten years, at a 10 percent discount rate, the present value of 200,000 dollars a year is about 1,229,000 dollars. That is the number your adviser is really selling, and the one you now test.

The two costs most models leave out

First, substance cost. A holding company that genuinely qualifies needs real directors, a local office or service, its own bank relationship, accounts and audit, and board meetings held where it lives. Say, hypothetically, 120,000 dollars a year. Second, the cost of failure. If the rate is denied later, you owe the difference plus interest and possibly a penalty, often years after the cash was distributed and spent.

Continue the example. Net annual benefit with substance: 200,000 dollars less 120,000 dollars, which is 80,000 dollars. Its ten-year present value at 10 percent is about 492,000 dollars, not 1,229,000. Now suppose you judge a 20 percent chance that the rate is denied after five years, with interest and penalty adding, hypothetically, 50 percent to the tax shortfall of 1,000,000 dollars. Expected cost: 20 percent of 1,500,000 dollars, which is 300,000 dollars, and it arrives in year 6, so its present value is about 186,000 dollars. Risk-adjusted value of the structure: roughly 492,000 less 186,000, about 306,000 dollars. A quarter of the headline.

Say that out loud now.

A treaty rate is worth the tax saved, less substance cost, less the expected cost of denial.

How it moves after-tax IRR

A second worked example. An investor puts 10,000,000 dollars of equity into a project that distributes 1,000,000 dollars a year for nine years and returns 15,000,000 dollars on sale in year 10, plus that year's 1,000,000 dollars. Assume, hypothetically, that the sale gain is taxed in the source country under the land rule whatever the structure, so the treaty touches only the annual distributions. At 25 percent withholding and no credit at home, the investor keeps 750,000 dollars a year. At 5 percent, 950,000 dollars. On these round numbers, the after-tax equity IRR rises by roughly 1.7 percentage points with the treaty, before substance cost. Subtract 120,000 dollars a year for substance and the gain falls to roughly 1 point.

Two lessons sit in that example. The treaty touches income far more than it touches the sale, because land gains usually stay taxable at source. And if the residence country gives a full credit for the withholding, the treaty's value to the investor can shrink toward zero, because a higher foreign tax would have been credited at home anyway. It then mostly helps cash timing and the investor whose home tax rate is low. Always ask: saved from whom?

The timing of the cash matters too

Even where the home credit would eventually neutralise a higher foreign withholding, the treaty can still be worth something, because withheld tax leaves at once while the credit arrives only when you file at home, often a year or more later. That is a cost of carry. On 200,000 dollars of extra withholding held for 18 months at a hypothetical 8 percent cost of capital, the carry is about 24,000 dollars a year. Small beside the headline, real beside zero. And if the extra foreign tax ever exceeds the credit cap, it is not timing at all: it is gone. Elias works that arithmetic on Day 5.

So when you read a structure proposal, put three numbers in a row before you look at anything else: the gross saving, the saving after the home credit, and the saving after substance cost and denial risk. The third is the only one you may underwrite. The first is the one that will be sold to you.

How the best do it

Disciplined cross-border investors decide structure from a two-column model: the claimed position and the denied position, both carried through to after-tax IRR, with the cost of substance as its own line. They do not adopt an intermediate company unless the risk-adjusted value clearly beats doing nothing. A small developer can copy the habit with one extra tab in the pro forma.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: on your personal balance sheet, an aggressive treaty position is a contingent liability. If the rate could be denied for open years, the tax at risk is money you may owe, and it should sit in your mind, and in your reserves, until those years close. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing the treaty at its headline saving and building the equity case on it. The control is a denied-rate scenario in every cross-border model, carried to after-tax IRR, with substance cost shown as a line.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets the residence-country credit. A lower foreign rate saves nothing if the home country would have credited the higher one and charged the difference anyway.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage and Elias called taxes after-tax leakage and warned that IRR can flatter a deal. A treaty position is exactly that kind of number: it looks like return, and part of it is only a probability.

Recap

Withholding comes off every distribution, so the treaty rate moves cash yield and after-tax IRR. Value a treaty position as tax saved, less the yearly cost of real substance, less the probability-weighted cost of denial, and check whether the home credit would have neutralised it anyway.

Next: Devika on The Rules: how a treaty is read, beneficial ownership, anti-abuse tests, and how Canada and Guyana approach treaties.
checklist: My model shows distributions before withholding, after withholding and after home tax.
I have priced the substance needed to qualify for each treaty rate.
I have a denied-rate scenario carried through to after-tax IRR.
I know whether the home country gives a credit that neutralises the foreign saving.
I know which income the treaty touches and which, like land gains, it does not.
I treat open-year treaty exposure as a contingent liability.
I adopt an intermediate company only if its risk-adjusted value clearly beats doing nothing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Withholding tax comes off the top of every distribution before the money leaves the source country, so a treaty rate moves cash yield and after-tax IRR every year. But a treaty rate is not free. Its value is the present value of the tax it saves, less the yearly cost of the substance needed to qualify, such as real directors, banking and accounts, less the probability-weighted cost of the rate being denied years later with interest and penalties. In my hypothetical example, a 200,000 dollar a year saving looked worth about 1.2 million dollars, but after substance cost and a modest chance of denial it was worth closer to 300,000. Two more checks. Land gains usually stay taxable where the land is, so the treaty mostly touches income, not the sale. And if my home country credits foreign tax fully, the lower rate may save me little. I model the claimed and the denied case side by side, every time.
terms: Withholding tax — tax deducted by the payer at source from a payment to a non-resident, before the money leaves the country.
Risk-adjusted value — the expected value of a benefit after deducting its costs and the probability-weighted cost of it failing.
Contingent liability — an obligation that may arise depending on a future event, such as a tax reassessment for open years.

hostile.q: Your returns jump once you add the holding company. How much of that is real?
hostile.a: I show you both. The headline saving is the withholding difference, but I deduct the yearly cost of the substance that makes the company qualify, and I carry a denied-rate case with interest and penalty. On a risk-adjusted basis the structure is worth about a quarter of the headline, and the investor case does not depend on it. If you prefer, underwrite at the domestic rate, and treat the treaty as upside.

title: Reading a Treaty: Beneficial Ownership, Anti-Abuse and the Land Clause
summary: A treaty is read in good faith by its ordinary meaning in context, alongside domestic law that it can override only to limit tax. Three clauses decide most developer cases: beneficial ownership for reduced withholding, the anti-abuse test, and the clause that keeps land and land-rich shares taxable where the land is. Two Systems compares how Canada and Guyana approach treaties.
body:
You read a treaty clause by clause, against domestic law, and three clauses decide most real estate cases: who beneficially owns the payment, whether the arrangement passes the anti-abuse test, and whether the gain is from land that stays taxable where it sits.

Recall

Q. What should a substance record contain for a board meeting?

A. The agenda and papers sent in advance, who attended and from where, what was discussed, what was decided and why, and signed minutes made at the time. Its value is that it is contemporaneous.

Q. In structure design, why is control mapped separately from ownership?

A. Because the person who owns shares and the person who makes decisions can differ, and tax residence, liability and lender consent often follow control rather than ownership.

Q. What is change control?

A. The written process for proposing, pricing, approving and recording any change to scope, cost or time before the work proceeds, so the budget and contract stay true.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a treaty is a legal text, and the person who reads it carefully usually wins. Developers hear that a treaty "allows" a rate. What it actually does is say that a rate may not exceed a figure for a defined recipient, holding a defined stake, who meets defined conditions. Read the conditions and you know whether to believe the claim. This lesson teaches concepts, not conclusions; every point must be verified against the primary source before you rely on it.

How a treaty is read

In plain English: start with the treaty's own words, in context, read honestly, then use the official commentary to understand them.

The professional framing: treaties are interpreted under international law principles of good faith and ordinary meaning in context and purpose, the approach set out in the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties. Courts often look at the commentary to the model convention the treaty follows, though how much weight they give it varies. Domestic law supplies meanings the treaty leaves undefined. And the relationship runs one way: a treaty can reduce or remove tax domestic law imposes, but it cannot impose one. Many countries implement treaties through a domestic statute, which sometimes says which prevails in a conflict [unverified — confirm independently].

Applied: when an adviser cites a treaty article, ask for four things. The article's text. The defined terms it relies on. The domestic provision it modifies. And any protocol or later amendment, because treaties are changed by protocols and, in many cases, by a multilateral instrument that inserts new clauses without rewriting the treaty itself.

Beneficial ownership

Reduced rates on dividends, interest and royalties usually apply only if the recipient is the beneficial owner. The core idea, as courts and commentary have developed it, is that the recipient has the right to use and enjoy the payment, unconstrained by a legal or contractual obligation to pass it to someone else. An agent, a nominee and a conduit usually fail. A holding company with real discretion, its own risks and its own decisions can pass, even if it later chooses to distribute.

A worked example, hypothetical. Company H in a treaty country receives 1,000,000 dollars of interest from a project company. Version one: H borrowed the money from its parent on terms requiring it to pay the parent back the same interest, a few days later, less a thin margin. H is close to a conduit and its claim is weak. Version two: H funded the loan from its own equity, holds several loans, decides its own reinvestment and has no back-to-back obligation. H looks like a beneficial owner. Same payment, same treaty, opposite answers, decided by facts about H.

The anti-abuse clause

Many treaties now contain a principal purpose test: a benefit is denied if obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, unless granting it would be in line with the object and purpose of the treaty. Some treaties, notably those of the United States, use a limitation-on-benefits clause instead, a set of objective tests about who owns and runs the claimant [unverified — confirm independently]. Domestic general anti-avoidance rules can apply too. Read the test as written; do not assume the familiar version.

Say that out loud now.

Beneficial ownership asks who may use the money; the principal purpose test asks why the arrangement exists.

The land clause

Almost every treaty lets the country where land sits tax gains on that land. Many go further and let it tax gains on shares of a company whose value comes mainly from land there, so selling the company instead of the building does not escape source tax. The threshold, the look-back period and any exceptions, such as for property in which a business is carried on, differ treaty by treaty.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A foreign holding company owns all the shares of a project company whose assets are 90 percent land and buildings in Country S. It sells the shares for a 5,000,000 dollar gain. If the treaty's land-rich share clause applies at, say, more than half of value from local real property, S may tax the 5,000,000 dollars as though the building were sold. If the treaty has no such clause, S's domestic law might still try, and the treaty might stop it. That single clause decides whether the exit is taxed at source.

Notice the timing question too. Land-rich tests are often measured at the time of sale or at any point in a look-back period, so a company that held mostly land a year before the sale may still be caught even if it later bought other assets. Read the period, not only the percentage.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

Conceptually, and to be verified against the primary source in each country: Canada has a large treaty network, mostly following the OECD model, implemented through domestic statutes, and has adopted changes through the multilateral instrument, including a principal purpose test in many treaties [unverified — confirm independently]. Its domestic law also contains a general anti-avoidance rule that courts have applied to treaty arrangements in some cases and declined to apply in others. Guyana has a much smaller network. It has been reported to have a treaty with Canada and to participate in a regional double taxation agreement among Caribbean Community states [unverified — confirm independently]. With fewer treaties, a Guyanese project paying abroad may more often face domestic withholding rates with no treaty relief at all, so domestic law does more of the work. Verify every one of these points against current primary sources before relying on any of them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on a summary of a treaty, a rate table or an adviser's sentence, instead of the clause, its defined terms and its later amendments. The control is a treaty position memo that quotes the operative text and every protocol, and is checked when either country announces a change.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the land rule covers only direct sales of buildings, and plans an exit by selling shares. Many treaties tax land-rich shares the same way.

Professional sign-off required: tax lawyer or tax adviser in each country, on the treaty position and the exit.

Callback

In Week 19, LEX taught that law has sources and a hierarchy, and that the text controls before commentary or custom. A treaty sits inside that hierarchy as a special kind of source, one that can only bend domestic tax downward, and the same habit applies: go to the text first.

Recap

Read a treaty in good faith by its words, in context, with commentary and domestic law alongside. Reduced withholding usually needs beneficial ownership; modern treaties add a principal purpose or limitation-on-benefits test; and land, often including land-rich shares, stays taxable where it sits.

Next: Elias on The Numbers: credit versus exemption, the credit cap and treaty withholding, worked step by step.
checklist: I have the operative treaty text, its defined terms and every protocol.
I know which domestic provision each clause modifies.
I have tested beneficial ownership against real facts, including back-to-back obligations.
I know whether the treaty has a principal purpose test or a limitation-on-benefits clause.
I know whether the treaty taxes gains on land-rich shares, and the threshold.
I have checked whether the multilateral instrument modified this treaty.
My treaty memo is reviewed whenever either country changes its rules.
head: Field checklist
speak: A treaty is read in good faith by its ordinary words, in context and purpose, with the official commentary and domestic law alongside, and it can only reduce tax that domestic law imposes. Three clauses decide most real estate cases. Beneficial ownership: a reduced withholding rate usually goes only to a recipient that can use and enjoy the payment, not one obliged to pass it on. Anti-abuse: many treaties now deny benefits where obtaining them was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, and some use objective limitation-on-benefits tests instead. And the land clause: the country where land sits can tax gains on it, and often on shares of land-rich companies too, so selling the company does not escape. Canada has a wide treaty network and has added anti-abuse clauses through a multilateral instrument; Guyana has far fewer treaties, so domestic rates do more of the work. Every point needs checking against the primary source.
terms: Beneficial owner — the recipient who has the right to use and enjoy a payment, without a legal or contractual duty to pass it on.
Principal purpose test — a treaty clause denying a benefit where obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, unless consistent with the treaty's object.
Land-rich share clause — a treaty rule letting the country where real property sits tax gains on shares deriving most of their value from that property.

hostile.q: Your exit plan is to sell the shares of the project company abroad. Why won't the source country tax that gain?
hostile.a: It may well tax it. The treaty we rely on has a land-rich share clause, and the project company's value is mostly local real property, so I have assumed the gain is taxable at source and modelled the exit that way. If the treaty or domestic law gives an exception, it is upside. I would rather show you the conservative case and be wrong in your favour.

title: Credit, Exemption and Withholding, Worked Step by Step
summary: Work one hypothetical income stream from a foreign building to its owner's home country under three treatments: no treaty, treaty with credit, and treaty with exemption. Then add the credit cap, which decides whether excess foreign tax is wasted. Every rate is hypothetical and chosen only to show the arithmetic.
body:
Follow one dollar of foreign profit all the way home, under credit and under exemption, and the treaty stops being a promise and becomes a number you can check.

Recall

Q. What does a treaty tie-breaker do?

A. When both countries treat the same person as resident under their own laws, it applies an ordered list of tests to give residence, for treaty purposes, to one country only.

Q. Why can a structure that is legal in its own jurisdiction still fail elsewhere?

A. Because each country applies its own law to the parts that touch it. A company valid where it was formed can still be resident, or have a permanent establishment, or be denied a treaty rate, somewhere else.

Q. What is a cost code?

A. A label tying each budget, commitment and invoice to a place in the work breakdown structure, so costs can be tracked against the estimate line by line.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when an adviser tells you a structure is "tax efficient", ask to see one year of income followed from top to bottom. If they cannot show it in a table, they have not done it. Today you build that table yourself, so you can check theirs. All rates here are hypothetical and chosen only to make the arithmetic visible; real rates must be verified against the primary source before you rely on them.

The setup

A company resident in Country R owns, through a subsidiary in Country S, an apartment building in S. The subsidiary earns 1,000,000 dollars of taxable profit. Country S corporate tax: a hypothetical 25 percent. Country S domestic withholding on dividends to non-residents: a hypothetical 20 percent. Treaty rate on dividends to a company holding a large stake: a hypothetical 5 percent. Country R corporate tax: a hypothetical 30 percent.

Step 1: tax in the source country

Profit 1,000,000 dollars, times 25 percent, equals 250,000 dollars of S corporate tax. After-tax profit: 750,000 dollars. The subsidiary pays all of it as a dividend.

Step 2: withholding

Without a treaty: 750,000 dollars times 20 percent equals 150,000 dollars withheld. The parent receives 600,000 dollars. With the treaty: 750,000 dollars times 5 percent equals 37,500 dollars. The parent receives 712,500 dollars. The treaty is already worth 112,500 dollars in cash this year.

Say that out loud now.

Corporate tax first, withholding second, home tax last, and the credit can never exceed the home tax on that income.

Step 3a: home country gives a credit

Suppose R taxes foreign dividends and gives a credit for foreign tax. There are two kinds of foreign tax here: the withholding, which the parent paid, and the underlying corporate tax, which the subsidiary paid. Some systems credit only the withholding. Others also give an indirect credit for underlying corporate tax when the parent holds a large enough stake. Which applies is a domestic-law question; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Case one, withholding credit only, with the treaty. R taxes the gross dividend of 750,000 dollars at 30 percent: 225,000 dollars. Credit for withholding: 37,500 dollars. R tax payable: 187,500 dollars. Total tax on the original 1,000,000 dollars: 250,000 plus 37,500 plus 187,500, which is 475,000 dollars. The parent keeps 525,000 dollars.

Case two, indirect credit as well. R grosses the dividend back up to the 1,000,000 dollars of pre-tax profit and taxes that at 30 percent: 300,000 dollars. Credits: 250,000 dollars of underlying tax plus 37,500 dollars of withholding, which is 287,500 dollars. R tax payable: 12,500 dollars. Total tax: 300,000 dollars, exactly R's rate. The parent keeps 700,000 dollars.

Step 3b: home country exempts the dividend

Suppose instead R exempts qualifying foreign dividends. R tax: zero. Total tax: 250,000 plus 37,500, which is 287,500 dollars. The parent keeps 712,500 dollars. Without the treaty, under exemption, it keeps 600,000 dollars.

Treatment, with treatyTotal taxParent keeps
Credit for withholding only475,000525,000
Credit including underlying tax300,000700,000
Exemption287,500712,500

Look at the second row. Under a full indirect credit, the treaty's lower withholding saves the parent almost nothing over time, because a higher withholding would also have been credited against R tax. Run it without the treaty: credits of 250,000 plus 150,000 equal 400,000 dollars against R tax of 300,000 dollars. R tax payable is zero, the parent keeps 600,000 dollars, and 100,000 dollars of credit is unused. That is the credit cap at work.

Step 4: the credit cap

Most credit systems limit the credit to the home tax on that foreign income. Foreign tax above that cap is wasted unless domestic law lets you carry it to another year. In the no-treaty case under full credit, 100,000 dollars was wasted. So the treaty's real value under a credit system is mostly the excess credit it prevents, here 100,000 dollars, plus earlier cash, not the full withholding difference.

Some systems let unused credit be carried back or forward a set number of years, or pooled across countries, so that excess from a high-tax source can shelter tax on income from a low-tax one. Others ring-fence each country or each type of income. The rule decides whether the 100,000 dollars is lost or merely delayed; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A second worked example: exemption with progression

An individual resident in R earns 100,000 dollars of foreign rent, exempt under a treaty, and 100,000 dollars of home salary. R uses exemption with progression: it ignores the rent but taxes the salary at the rate that would apply to 200,000 dollars. If, hypothetically, the average rate on 200,000 dollars is 30 percent and on 100,000 dollars is 22 percent, his home tax is 30,000 dollars instead of 22,000. Exemption did not make the rent invisible; it raised the rate on everything else.

Reading the result

Now read the table the way a lender or investor would. The spread between the worst and best rows, 525,000 against 712,500 dollars, is 187,500 dollars a year on 1,000,000 dollars of profit, nearly a fifth of it, and it came from the home country's relief mechanism, not from the treaty rate. That is why Elias insists the home adviser signs off before the source adviser's structure is adopted. Most mistakes in cross-border modelling sit in the home column, because the people designing the foreign structure rarely practise home tax.

And check the units at every line. Corporate tax is on profit. Withholding is on the dividend, which is after-tax profit. Indirect credit grosses the dividend back up to pre-tax profit. Mixing those bases, for example applying withholding to the 1,000,000 dollars instead of the 750,000 dollar dividend, overstates the tax by a third of the withholding and is the commonest arithmetic error in this area.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a model that counts the treaty's withholding saving in full when the home credit would have neutralised most of it, so equity is promised a return the structure never produces. The control is to run every distribution through source tax, withholding and home tax, with the credit cap, in one table.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner applies the home rate to the net dividend and forgets the gross-up for underlying tax, or forgets the cap, and gets a number that is wrong in both directions at once.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in each country, on the credit or exemption mechanism and the cap.

Callback

Three lessons back, Sage priced a treaty rate against its substance cost and denial risk. This table is the engine under that price: it shows how much of the headline saving the home country would have taken back anyway.

Recap

Source corporate tax first, then withholding, then home tax with its credit or exemption. Under a full credit, a lower withholding mainly prevents wasted excess credit; under exemption, it is a direct saving, though progression may raise tax elsewhere. One table, every time.

Next: Elias on The Room: defending a treaty position to a buyer's tax diligence team.
checklist: I follow every distribution through source tax, withholding and home tax in one table.
I know whether my home country credits withholding only or underlying tax as well.
I know the credit cap and whether excess credit can be carried to another year.
I know whether exemption is given with progression.
I have computed the treaty's value as excess credit prevented, not just rate difference.
Every rate in my table is labelled and sourced.
Advisers in both countries have checked the mechanism.
head: Field checklist
speak: Follow one year of foreign profit home in four steps. First, source-country corporate tax on the profit. Second, withholding on the dividend that leaves, at the domestic rate or a lower treaty rate. Third, home-country tax. Under a credit system the home country taxes the dividend and subtracts foreign tax, sometimes only the withholding and sometimes the underlying corporate tax too, after grossing the dividend back up. Under exemption it taxes nothing, though exemption with progression can raise the rate on my other income. Fourth, the credit cap: most systems will not credit more than their own tax on that income, so excess foreign tax is wasted. That cap changes the treaty's value. Under a full credit, a lower withholding rate mostly prevents wasted credit rather than saving its whole difference. In my hypothetical table the parent kept 525,000, 700,000 or 712,500 dollars of a million, depending on the mechanism alone.
terms: Indirect credit — a credit at home for the underlying corporate tax a foreign subsidiary paid, available in some systems for large shareholdings.
Credit cap — the limit, usually the home tax on the foreign income, above which foreign tax cannot be credited.
Exemption with progression — relief that exempts foreign income but counts it in setting the tax rate on the taxpayer's other income.

hostile.q: Your table shows the parent keeping 712,500 dollars. Under which home-country rule, exactly?
hostile.a: Under exemption of qualifying foreign dividends, which my home adviser has confirmed applies to this shareholding, with the treaty rate on withholding. I have also shown the credit cases, because if the exemption conditions were not met, the parent would keep 525,000 or 700,000 dollars depending on whether the underlying tax is credited. The underwriting uses the lowest of the three.

title: Defending a Treaty Position to a Buyer's Tax Diligence Team
summary: A buyer's tax advisers will test every treaty claim in your structure before they price the deal. The scene shows what to bring, what to say, what never to say, the question behind their questions, and when to stop talking. Your goal is not to win the argument; it is to show the position was built on facts.
body:
In tax diligence, the buyer is not asking whether your treaty position is clever; they are asking how much of it they would inherit if it fails, and you answer with documents, not adjectives.

Recall

Q. What is a conduit company?

A. An entity that receives income only to pass it on, without real discretion over it. Conduits usually fail beneficial-ownership tests and lose reduced treaty rates.

Q. What does a structure memo need beyond a chart of boxes?

A. The reason for each entity, the flow of funds, who controls each one, the sequencing, and the six-lens consequences, so a reader can see why it is built that way.

Q. Why do owners care about exclusions in a contractor's scope?

A. Because every excluded item is a cost the owner still carries; if no other package or budget line picks it up, it surfaces later as an unplanned change.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you sell a stabilised building held through a cross-border structure, the buyer may acquire your companies, not just the building. If it does, it inherits their tax history, including every treaty rate they have claimed. Its advisers will find any weakness, and either cut the price, demand an indemnity, or insist on buying the asset instead of the shares. How you handle that meeting can move the price by more than the tax at stake, because uncertainty is priced worse than a known number.

The scene

A conference room. Across the table: the buyer's tax partner, a junior who takes notes, and the buyer's deal lead. Your side: you and your tax adviser. On the table is your holding structure: a project company in Country S, owned by a holding company in Country T, owned by your company at home. Hypothetically, the holding company has received 1,000,000 dollars of dividends a year for six years at a treaty rate of 5 percent instead of a domestic 20 percent.

The tax partner opens: "Walk us through why the T company qualifies for the 5 percent rate."

The lines to say

Bottom line first: "It qualifies on three grounds: residence, beneficial ownership and the treaty's anti-abuse test. Here is the evidence for each, in that order." Then hand over the treaty position memo and the substance file. Residence: the certificate from T for each year. Beneficial ownership: the company's own bank mandate, signed by its resident directors; its other investments; the absence of any back-to-back obligation; minutes showing it decided on each distribution. Anti-abuse: the documented business reasons for being in T, written before the first dividend.

When they probe a weakness, acknowledge, bridge, answer, Kema's sequence from Week 6. "You're right that the directors are provided by a service firm. What matters is that they decide, and here are three occasions when they declined our proposal and held cash instead." Then stop.

Say that out loud now.

It qualifies on residence, beneficial ownership and the anti-abuse test, and here is the evidence for each.

The lines never to say

Never say "everyone does this." It invites the reply that everyone gets audited. Never say "the authority has never challenged it." Absence of an audit is not acceptance. Never call the position "aggressive" or "safe"; both are opinions, and the first one will be quoted in a price-reduction memo. Never guess at a fact you do not know. Say, "I'll confirm that by Friday," write it down, and deliver it.

The question behind the question

Every question in this room is really one question: how much could this cost us, and how likely is it? When the partner asks about board meetings, she is estimating the probability of a beneficial-ownership challenge. When she asks how many years are still open to audit, she is sizing the exposure. Help her size it honestly and you take control of the number.

A worked example, hypothetical. Six years at 1,000,000 dollars, a 15 percent rate difference: 150,000 dollars a year. If four years remain open, the exposure before interest is 600,000 dollars. If interest and penalty add, say, 40 percent, about 840,000 dollars. A buyer who cannot size it may discount the price by more than that, or walk. A seller who has already sized it can offer a specific, capped indemnity for those years, or an escrow of 840,000 dollars released as each year closes, and keep the price.

A second worked example. The buyer proposes buying the building, not the shares, to avoid inheriting the history. Hypothetically, an asset sale triggers transfer tax and recapture inside the project company that a share sale would have avoided, together 1,500,000 dollars. Now you can compare: an 840,000 dollar capped indemnity against a 1,500,000 dollar change of deal form. The numbers, not the argument, settle it.

The answer to the hardest question

Sooner or later the partner asks: "If this structure were set up today, would you use it?" It is the question behind every other question, because it tests whether you believe your own file. Do not dodge it. If the honest answer is yes, say so and say why, in one sentence. If the honest answer is that rules have tightened since the structure was built, say that too: "The law has moved since we set this up, which is why I have sized the open years and offered to carry them." Candour on a known weakness buys credibility on everything else you have said, and a buyer who catches you shading one answer will discount all the others.

When to stay silent

After you hand over the substance file, stop talking and let them read. Silence while a reviewer reads tells them you expect the documents to speak. Do not narrate the minutes. Do not pre-empt a criticism they have not raised.

The same applies after you name a number. If you have proposed an escrow of 840,000 dollars, say it once and wait. The first person to fill the silence after a number usually moves it, and it should not be you.

A third moment for silence: when the buyer's team confer among themselves. Let them. Whatever you say into that pause will be heard as nerves, and they are deciding how much to worry, which you have already shaped with the file.

Holding your state

The tax partner's job is to make you uncomfortable about risk so her client pays less. Expect it, and do not take it personally. Slow your speech. Keep your hands still on the table. If you feel the urge to defend, ask a question instead: "Which fact would change your view?" It turns an attack into a list.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arriving with a confident story and no file, so the buyer's team prices the worst case. The control is a diligence-ready treaty file, prepared as part of the annual close, not the week before a sale.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner argues the law with the buyer's tax partner. She is not a judge. Give her facts to size the risk and a mechanism, indemnity or escrow, to allocate it.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser and transaction lawyer, on the indemnity, escrow and deal form.

Callback

Four lessons back, in the composite case, the conduit company's file could not be rebuilt after five years of pass-through dividends. This room is where that matters most. A substance record built at the time is the only thing that answers the buyer's question, and no one can write it later.

Recap

In tax diligence, lead with the three grounds and the evidence, acknowledge weaknesses briefly, size the exposure with the buyer, and offer a specific mechanism to allocate it. Say less than you want to, and let the file speak.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on treaties, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: I have a diligence-ready treaty file updated at each annual close.
I can state the three grounds for each treaty claim in one sentence.
I know how many years remain open to audit in each country.
I have sized the exposure, with interest and penalty, before the buyer does.
I have a proposal ready for a capped indemnity or escrow.
I have compared the cost of a share sale indemnity against an asset sale.
I will say “I'll confirm by Friday” instead of guessing.
head: Field checklist
speak: When I sell a building through a cross-border structure, the buyer may buy my companies and inherit their tax history, including every treaty rate they claimed. Its tax team will test those claims. I open with the bottom line: the holding company qualifies on residence, beneficial ownership and the anti-abuse test, and here is the evidence for each. Then I hand over the file and stop talking. If they find a weakness, I acknowledge it, bridge, and answer with a fact. I never say everyone does this, never say it has never been challenged, and never call the position safe or aggressive. The question behind every question is how much this could cost and how likely it is. So I size it with them: open years, rate difference, interest and penalty. Then I offer a capped indemnity or an escrow released as each year closes. A sized risk is priced far better than an unknown one.
terms: Tax diligence — a buyer's review of a target's tax history and positions to identify and price inherited exposure.
Tax indemnity — a seller's contractual promise to pay the buyer for defined pre-sale tax liabilities, usually capped and time-limited.
Escrow — money held by a neutral party under agreed terms, released to one side or the other as conditions are met.

hostile.q: If we buy the shares and the treaty rate is denied for open years, why should we carry that?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. I have sized the exposure for the open years, including interest and penalty, and I will give you a specific indemnity for it, capped at that amount, or put that amount in escrow to be released as each year closes. That leaves you with a clean company and me with the risk of my own position, which is where it belongs.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 57 Review: Treaties, Tie-Breakers, Relief and Beneficial Ownership
summary: Six questions test the week: what treaties do, tie-breakers, credit versus exemption, the credit cap, beneficial ownership and anti-abuse tests. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical treaty memo, and a boardroom drill asks you to explain treaties in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a treaty only limits tax domestic law already imposes, and only for a resident who is the real owner of the income, has a real reason to be where it is, and can prove both.

Recall

Q. What three costs reduce the headline value of a treaty rate?

A. The yearly cost of the substance needed to qualify, the probability-weighted cost of the rate being denied with interest and penalty, and any saving the home country's credit would have given anyway.

Q. What is the purpose of sequencing in structure design?

A. To order transfers, financings and incorporations so that each step gets the intended tax and legal result, because the same steps in a different order can produce a different outcome.

Q. What happens when scope changes without change control?

A. Work proceeds without an agreed price or time, the budget and contract stop matching reality, and the dispute arrives later with weaker records.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, treaties sit under every cross-border distribution you will ever make. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can test any treaty claim an adviser makes. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four jobs a tax treaty does.

Answer: It allocates taxing rights between source and residence country, caps withholding on cross-border payments, requires the residence country to relieve double tax by credit or exemption, and enables information exchange and dispute resolution between the authorities.

Question 2. Can a treaty create a tax?

Answer: No. A treaty can only reduce or remove tax that domestic law imposes. If domestic law does not tax a payment, a treaty cannot make it taxable.

Question 3. In what order does the individual tie-breaker run?

Answer: Permanent home available; then centre of vital interests; then habitual abode; then nationality; then agreement between the authorities. Each test is reached only if the one before it does not decide.

Question 4. Why can a lower treaty withholding rate save little under a full credit system?

Answer: Because a higher foreign tax would have been credited against home tax anyway, up to the credit cap. The treaty then mostly prevents wasted excess credit and improves cash timing.

Question 5. What is beneficial ownership, and what usually fails it?

Answer: The right to use and enjoy a payment, free of a legal or contractual duty to pass it on. Agents, nominees and conduits with back-to-back obligations usually fail.

Question 6. What does a principal purpose test ask?

Answer: Whether obtaining the treaty benefit was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement. If so, the benefit is denied unless granting it fits the treaty's object and purpose.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Elias framed treaties as agreements that only restrict, with tie-breakers, credit and exemption. Ford and Cole took a composite case of a conduit company that lost its rate, giving Rule 57. Sage priced a treaty position as saving, less substance cost, less expected denial. Devika taught how treaties are read, with beneficial ownership, anti-abuse and the land clause, and compared Canada and Guyana. Elias worked the credit and exemption arithmetic. Elias then defended a treaty position to a buyer's diligence team.

The Red Pen

Find the defects in this hypothetical treaty memo before reading on.

Memo: Dividend route. Holdco in Country T is entitled to the 5 percent treaty rate on dividends from Propco in Country S because it holds a certificate of residence from T. Holdco will receive dividends quarterly and pay them to the parent within five days under the shareholder loan agreement. The treaty rate saves 150,000 dollars a year, which we have added to investor distributions. On exit, Holdco will sell Propco's shares, so the gain falls outside the land article and is not taxable in S. Directors: one nominee from a service firm. Prepared from the treaty rate table, current edition.

The defects. First, a certificate of residence is treated as enough; the memo never addresses beneficial ownership or the anti-abuse test. Second, the five-day onward payment under a shareholder loan is a back-to-back obligation, the mark of a conduit. Third, the saving is added to investor distributions with no denied-rate case and no check of the home credit. Fourth, the exit claim ignores the possibility of a land-rich share clause; selling Propco's shares may be taxed in S. Fifth, a single nominee director undermines decisions being made in T. Sixth, the memo relies on a rate table, not the treaty text, its protocols or any multilateral changes. Seventh, there is no date, adviser name or sign-off in either country.

Then write the corrected memo in four lines. Holdco's claim rests on residence, beneficial ownership and the principal purpose test, with the evidence for each attached. Holdco holds dividends at its own directors' discretion, with no onward obligation. Investor distributions are modelled at the domestic rate, with the treaty saving shown separately as upside after the home credit. The exit is modelled as taxable in S unless the treaty text, checked with protocols, says otherwise. Notice how much shorter the honest memo is: most defects are claims that should not have been made.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why should I believe our adviser when she says the treaty gives us 5 percent?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "A treaty is an agreement between two countries that limits tax domestic law already imposes. It caps the withholding on our dividends, but only for a company that is resident in the treaty country, is the beneficial owner of the dividends, and passes the anti-abuse test. Beneficial owner means it can use the money, not just pass it on. The anti-abuse test asks whether getting the treaty rate was one of the main reasons for the arrangement. So I want three things from the adviser: the treaty text and any amendments, the facts showing our holding company really decides and is not a pipe, and the business reason for its location, written down before the first payment. Then I want the model run two ways, at the treaty rate and at the domestic rate, and I want to know whether our home country's credit would have given us most of the saving anyway. And I assume the exit stays taxable where the land is unless proven otherwise."

Notice what the model answer does not do. It never quotes a rate as a fact, never names a country, and never claims the structure is safe. It describes what has to be true and how to check it. That is the posture of an owner who uses advisers rather than being used by them, and it holds whatever treaty you are reading.

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all three conditions? Did you mention the denied-rate case and the home credit? Did you finish inside two minutes?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is accepting a treaty rate as a fact rather than a conclusion. The control: no treaty rate enters a model until its three conditions are documented and the denied case is shown.

The beginner's mistake

Memorising rates instead of conditions. Rates change by protocol; conditions decide whether you get any rate at all.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: before trusting your own case, ask how cases like it usually turn out. For treaty claims, the reference class is clear. Thin intermediate companies tend to lose on audit, and the ones that survive had real substance from day one.

Recap

Treaties restrict, tie-breakers assign residence, relief comes by credit or exemption subject to a cap, and reduced rates need beneficial ownership and a defensible purpose. Rule 57 keeps treaty claims tied to real ownership, control and decisions.

head: The six questions
speak: Treaties this week came down to one sentence: a treaty only limits tax that domestic law already imposes, and only for a resident who is the real owner of the income and has a real reason to be where it is. Treaties allocate taxing rights, cap withholding, require relief by credit or exemption, and let authorities cooperate. When two countries both claim a person, the tie-breaker runs permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, then agreement. Under a credit system, the credit is capped at home tax on the income, so a lower foreign rate often saves less than it seems. Reduced withholding usually requires beneficial ownership, meaning the recipient can use the money rather than pass it on, and many treaties add a principal purpose test. Land, and often land-rich shares, stays taxable where it sits. Rule 57: never claim a treaty rate through an entity that does not genuinely own, control and decide.
terms: Mutual agreement procedure — the treaty process through which the two tax authorities consult to resolve double taxation or disputes over the treaty's application.
Protocol — an amending instrument that changes an existing treaty's text, often years after the treaty was signed.
Multilateral instrument — a single agreement that modifies many bilateral treaties at once, for example to add anti-abuse clauses.

hostile.q: You say the treaty saves us 150,000 dollars a year. Prove it is real.
hostile.a: I will show it three ways. First, the treaty text and amendments, and the facts on residence, beneficial ownership and purpose. Second, the model at the treaty rate and at the domestic rate, so you see the downside. Third, the home-country tax on the same dividends, because if our credit would have covered the higher rate, most of that saving disappears. Until all three are on the table, I treat the saving as upside, not underwriting.
